source_evidence.observation: The source says that f ≍ g denotes equivalence of functions up to constant factors.
The source defines f ≍ g by the existence of positive constants c and C satisfying c f(x) ≤ g(x) ≤ C f(x) for all x, or sometimes for all sufficiently large x.

source_evidence.anchor: Final sentence beginning 'For similar one-sided inequalities'
source_evidence.observation: The source introduces f ≲ g and f ≳ g for the analogous one-sided comparisons that hold up to constant factors.

binders: f and g are comparable scalar-valued functions on a common, informally specified domain; in the motivating example they are functions of N (PDF page 3/printed page 14, footnote 1, parenthetical 'functions of N in this particular example').
x ranges over the common domain of f and g (PDF page 3/printed page 14, footnote 1, displayed inequalities involving f(x) and g(x)).
c and C are existentially chosen positive constants, uniform in x (PDF page 3/printed page 14, footnote 1, sentence beginning 'Precisely').
hypotheses: The values f(x) and g(x) lie in a setting where multiplication by positive constants and order comparisons are meaningful (PDF page 3/printed page 14, footnote 1, inequality c f(x) ≤ g(x) ≤ C f(x)).
conclusions: The notation f ≍ g means that there exist positive constants c and C such that c f(x) ≤ g(x) ≤ C f(x) for all x, or, depending on context, for all sufficiently large x (PDF page 3/printed page 14, footnote 1, sentence beginning 'Precisely').

The notation f ≲ g denotes the analogous one-sided upper comparison up to a positive constant factor, namely f(x) ≤ C g(x), with the same all-x or sufficiently-large-x scope convention (PDF page 3/printed page 14, footnote 1, final sentence on 'similar one-sided inequalities').

The notation f ≳ g denotes the analogous one-sided lower comparison up to a positive constant factor, namely c g(x) ≤ f(x), with the same all-x or sufficiently-large-x scope convention (PDF page 3/printed page 14, footnote 1, final sentence on 'similar one-sided inequalities').
definitions_and_conventions: The symbol ≍ expresses two-sided comparison up to positive multiplicative constants, not equality or asymptotic ratio one (PDF page 3/printed page 14, footnote 1, first two sentences).
The constants c and C are strictly positive (PDF page 3/printed page 14, footnote 1, phrase 'positive constants c, C').
The constants are chosen once for the comparison and do not vary with x (PDF page 3/printed page 14, footnote 1, existential constants followed by an inequality holding for all x).
The symbol ≲ expresses the corresponding one-sided 'bounded above up to a constant factor' relation (PDF page 3/printed page 14, footnote 1, final sentence).
The symbol ≳ expresses the corresponding one-sided 'bounded below up to a constant factor' relation (PDF page 3/printed page 14, footnote 1, final sentence).

The source allows both a global interpretation, valid for all x, and an eventual interpretation, valid for all sufficiently large x (PDF page 3/printed page 14, footnote 1, phrase 'or sometimes for all sufficiently large x').
implicit_context: In the immediately motivating use, the functions depend on the natural-number parameter N, but the notation footnote is phrased generically in terms of functions and x (PDF page 3/printed page 14, footnote 1, parenthetical remark and subsequent inequality).

The threshold implicit in 'sufficiently large x' is not part of the notation and may depend on the compared functions and context, while c and C remain uniform beyond it (PDF page 3/printed page 14, footnote 1, phrase 'for all sufficiently large x').

The footnote defines only comparison notation; neighboring claims about probabilities, normal approximation, binomial coefficients, or rates in N are not conclusions of this task (PDF page 3/printed page 14, structural separation of footnote 1 from the main text).

details: The lower comparison is c f(x) ≤ g(x) and the upper comparison is g(x) ≤ C f(x) (PDF page 3/printed page 14, footnote 1, sentence beginning 'Precisely').
Both inequalities must hold with positive constants fixed independently of x (PDF page 3/printed page 14, footnote 1, same sentence).
One permitted reading requires the comparison for every x in the domain (PDF page 3/printed page 14, footnote 1, phrase 'for all x').

The source also sometimes uses the notation for an eventual comparison holding only for all sufficiently large x (PDF page 3/printed page 14, footnote 1, phrase 'or sometimes for all sufficiently large x').
The notation f ≲ g retains only the upper comparison of f by g up to a positive constant factor (PDF page 3/printed page 14, footnote 1, final sentence introducing similar one-sided inequalities).
The notation f ≳ g retains only the lower comparison of f by g up to a positive constant factor (PDF page 3/printed page 14, footnote 1, final sentence introducing similar one-sided inequalities).

undebatable_constraints: The two-sided notation is f ≍ g (PDF page 3/printed page 14, footnote 1).
There must exist two positive constants c and C (PDF page 3/printed page 14, footnote 1, sentence beginning 'Precisely').
The exact two-sided inequalities are c f(x) ≤ g(x) ≤ C f(x) (PDF page 3/printed page 14, footnote 1, sentence beginning 'Precisely').
The constants are uniform over the x-values within the chosen scope (PDF page 3/printed page 14, footnote 1, existential constants followed by universal validity).
The scope may be all x or, in some uses, all sufficiently large x (PDF page 3/printed page 14, footnote 1, sentence beginning 'Precisely').
The symbols f ≲ g and f ≳ g denote analogous one-sided comparisons up to constant factors (PDF page 3/printed page 14, footnote 1, final sentence).
The notation does not mean literal equality, equality of limits, or that f(x)/g(x) tends to one (PDF page 3/printed page 14, footnote 1, characterization as equivalence only up to constant factors).
No neighboring probability, Berry–Esseen, Gaussian, binomial, or asymptotic-rate claim is part of this notation contract (PDF page 3/printed page 14, footnote 1 as a separate notation note).

ambiguities.evidence: PDF page 3/printed page 14, footnote 1 calls them functions, notes only that they are functions of N in the particular example, and writes ordered scalar inequalities without declaring types.
ambiguities.impact: A formal version must choose an ordered scalar codomain and a domain equipped with an interpretation of 'sufficiently large'.

ambiguities.issue: The notation is explicitly context-dependent between global and eventual comparison.

ambiguities.impact: The bare symbols ≍, ≲, and ≳ do not by themselves determine whether the formal relation should be global or eventual.

ambiguities.issue: The one-sided inequalities are described as analogous but are not written explicitly in the source.
ambiguities.evidence: PDF page 3/printed page 14, footnote 1 states only, 'For similar one-sided inequalities that hold up to constant factors, we use notation f ≲ g and f ≳ g.'
ambiguities.impact: Their standard orientations can be reconstructed as upper and lower comparison respectively, but a formal contract should record that this expansion is implicit rather than displayed verbatim.

contract_plain_english: The notation f ≍ g says that f and g stay within fixed positive constant multiples of one another: there are c,C>0 with c f(x)≤g(x)≤C f(x), either for every x or, in some contexts, for all sufficiently large x. The symbols f≲g and f≳g denote the corresponding one-sided upper and lower comparisons (PDF page 3/printed page 14, footnote 1).
